title: Notta AI: Meeting Notes With an On-Device Option
description: Notta AI records, transcribes and summarises meetings across Zoom, Meet and Teams, with an on-device transcription mode and an MCP server for agents.
content:
# Notta AI: Meeting Notes With an On-Device Option

Meeting transcription is a solved problem in the narrow sense: audio in, text out, and a summary on top. What separates the tools now is everything around that core — how the audio gets captured, where it is processed, what happens to it afterwards, and who is allowed to see it. Notta's feature list reads like an answer to those four questions rather than to the transcription question itself.

## Five ways in

The capture options are the first sign that this is built for real organisations rather than demos:

- **Online Meeting Recorder** — a bot joins the call
- **Bot-free Meeting Recorder** — records on your device, no bot in the participant list
- **Upload and Link** — audio, video files, or a YouTube link
- **Screen Recording** — screen, audio and camera
- **Notta Memo** — a physical device you stick on your phone to record calls and meetings

The bot-free mode exists because a visible bot changes the room. In sales calls, clinical conversations and anything with an external party, a recorder joining the meeting is a disclosure problem, and in some organisations it is simply prohibited. Offering both modes is the correct response, and the physical memo device is an unusual extension of the same idea: capture without altering the setting.

## Where the audio goes

[[link:/tools/485|Notta AI]] offers on-device transcription, where audio is processed locally and nothing leaves the machine. That is the single most consequential feature on the page for regulated industries, because it moves the tool out of the category of "third-party processor" and into "local software" for that step.

The rest of the security story is conventional but complete: SOC 2, ISO 27001, GDPR and HIPAA. Those certifications are the price of entry for healthcare and enterprise sales, not a differentiator, but their presence tells you which buyers the product is aimed at.

Transcription itself covers real-time, bilingual (two languages at once) and bilingual translation with the original and translation side by side. Bilingual transcription is a genuinely useful feature that most competitors treat as an afterthought — meetings where one side speaks English and the other does not are common and badly served.

## After the meeting

Summaries and action items are table stakes. The more interesting additions are cross-meeting Q&A, which lets you ask questions across all your meetings rather than one at a time, meeting infographics for sharing outcomes visually, a document builder that outputs PDF, Word, Excel and slides, follow-up email drafts, and Slack message drafts.

Cross-meeting Q&A is the feature that changes the tool from a recorder into a memory. Asking "what did we promise this client across the last six calls" is a different question from "summarise this call", and it is the one people actually have.

There is also an MCP server and CLI, which puts meeting context within reach of an agent. That is the same architectural bet Frase makes: the product expects to be read by software, not only by a person.

One integration deserves separate mention: the calendar connections. Pulling meeting titles and attendees from Google Calendar or Outlook is what turns a folder of recordings into a searchable history organised by who was in the room, and it is the difference between transcription and recall.

The desktop app and Chrome extension also matter more than they appear to. A browser tab can capture audio from a call that no bot is allowed to join, which is the practical answer for organisations that block meeting bots outright.

The upload path is the one that gets overlooked. Feeding it a podcast episode or a recorded interview turns the tool into a research instrument rather than a meeting accessory, and the document builder then emits the same content as Word, Excel or slides — which is what makes a transcript reusable instead of an archive nobody opens again.

## The integrations and the audience

Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, Webex, Slack, Notion, Salesforce, HubSpot, Google Calendar, Outlook, Google Drive and Zapier. The named audiences — consultants, sales, customer success, media and podcasting, education, agencies — are all people whose work output is partly conversational.

The trade-off across that breadth is depth. A tool that records, transcribes, translates, summarises, builds documents, drafts emails and answers questions across meetings is not going to be the best at any single one. If your only need is accurate transcription of clean audio, [[link:/tools/11|Whisper]] does that locally and free. If you need speaker-labelled summaries delivered to a CRM, the integrated route is worth the compromise.

What Notta has that most competitors lack is a coherent answer to "where does the audio go", with an on-device path and the certifications to back the cloud path. For anyone whose meetings contain material they are not allowed to send to a vendor, that is not a feature comparison — it is the whole decision.
tldr: Notta AI is a meeting note-taker that transcribes, summarises and extracts action items, with five ways to capture audio including a bot-free device recorder and an on-device transcription mode where audio never leaves the machine. It carries SOC 2, ISO 27001, GDPR and HIPAA, integrates with Zoom, Meet, Teams and Webex, and ships an MCP server and CLI so an agent can read meeting context.
